title: Integration
intro: Integration is the highest-weight domain on the CCAR-P exam because it is where Claude solutions meet real systems: tools, credentials, retrieval pipelines, protocols, and telemetry. The exam tests it almost entirely through scenario judgment — you are given a company, a design, and a constraint, and asked to spot the gap or pick the mechanism that fits. Expect questions that reward matching the mechanism to the workload (data shape, query pattern, SLA, corpus volatility) and penalize both under-engineering and over-engineering.

objectives.objective: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
objectives.explanation:
An agent's tool configuration is part of its prompt: every tool definition — name, description, parameter schema — is injected into context and competes for the model's attention. As the tool catalog grows, two costs compound. First, token cost: dozens or hundreds of definitions consume context on every request before any work happens. Second, selection accuracy: the more tools the model must choose among, especially when they overlap, the more often it picks the wrong one or passes malformed arguments.

Capability bloat is also a security problem. Every tool an agent holds is attack surface: a prompt injection or model error can only misuse capabilities the agent actually has. A generic 'run any SQL' tool, or auto-generating a tool per API endpoint, grants far more capability than any task requires. The evaluation question an architect asks is not 'what might this agent someday need' but 'what does this agent's job require' — then scope tools to that.

The practical remedies are curation and description quality. Curate a minimal, non-overlapping tool set per agent, consolidating tools that do the same job into one canonical capability. Then treat tool descriptions as prompt engineering: state what the tool does, when to use it instead of its neighbors, and what each parameter means. Many 'the model keeps calling the wrong tool' problems are fixed by rewriting descriptions, not by changing models or adding rules to the system prompt.
objectives.whyItMatters: In production, bloated tool catalogs quietly degrade every request: higher cost, slower prompt processing, more wrong-tool calls that surface as user-visible failures, and a wider blast radius when something goes wrong. Because tool sets grow one reasonable-sounding addition at a time, unreviewed catalogs drift toward bloat by default — architects are the control point that keeps agents scoped to their actual job.

examples.title: The 45-tool support agent
examples.body: A retailer's support agent accumulated 45 tools across returns, inventory, pricing, and marketing. Wrong-tool calls rose and token costs doubled. The team considered a bigger model and a longer rulebook in the system prompt, but both treat symptoms: any model's selection accuracy drops as overlapping options multiply, and more instructions add tokens on top of the bloat. The right move was pruning to the tools the support workflows actually use and merging overlapping search tools into one canonical version. Wrong-tool calls fell without touching the model.

examples.title: The generic SQL tool
examples.body: A hospital scheduling agent design included an 'execute_sql' tool so future needs would never require new development. The security review replaced it with two narrow tools, find_slot and reschedule_appointment. The reasoning: the generic tool exposed the entire schema, including patient data unrelated to scheduling, and a prompt injection could weaponize it. Narrow tools enforce least privilege deterministically — the agent physically cannot express operations outside its job, no matter what enters its context.

pitfalls: Fixing wrong-tool selection by upgrading the model — selection accuracy degrades with catalog size for any model, so the catalog, not the model, is usually the problem.
Adding prompt rules ('never use tool X for Y') instead of removing the ambiguity — instructions are probabilistic and add tokens; consolidation removes the ambiguity deterministically.
Granting capabilities for hypothetical future needs — unused capability is pure attack surface with zero present value; add tools when the need is real.
Splitting tools into many narrow variants to 'help' the model — more near-duplicate options increases selection ambiguity; the goal is fewer, clearer choices, not more precise ones.
Writing tool descriptions like internal API stubs — the model chooses tools based on the descriptions, so vague descriptions cause wrong calls even in a small, well-scoped catalog.

objectives.objective: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
objectives.explanation:
The foundational rule is that the model is never the authorization boundary. Claude is a non-deterministic component: prompt instructions like 'only discuss this customer's data' can be bypassed by prompt injection, jailbreaks, or plain model error. Authorization must be enforced deterministically in the systems the agent calls — if the agent's credential can read every record, then every record is in the blast radius of a manipulated session, regardless of what the prompt says.

The most common gap pattern is the shared service account: one machine identity with broad access serving all users, with the user's identity mentioned only in the prompt. This breaks authorization (the API cannot enforce per-user scope) and breaks auditability (logs attribute every action to the same account). The fix is per-user scoped credentials — exchange the authenticated user's session for a token carrying that user's entitlements and propagate it on every downstream call. For remote MCP servers, OAuth is the standard pattern: each user authorizes the server, which then acts within that user's scope.

The second key pattern is the confused deputy: an agent holding powerful credentials while processing untrusted content (emails, reviews, web pages, documents). Injected instructions in that content can drive the agent to misuse its privileges. Defenses layer — input filtering, model hardening, least-privilege tools — but for consequential or irreversible actions (payments, refunds, sending messages, deleting data), the load-bearing control must be deterministic and outside the model: scoped credentials that make the action impossible, policy checks in code, or human approval.
objectives.whyItMatters: Agent integrations concentrate risk: one over-privileged credential behind a conversational interface exposed to untrusted input is a breach waiting for a cleverly crafted message. Regulators and auditors increasingly ask exactly the questions this objective covers — who accessed what, under whose authority, and what prevents the AI from exceeding it — and retrofitting per-user authorization into a shipped agent is far costlier than designing it in.

examples.title: From shared account to scoped tokens
examples.body: A clinician assistant used one service account with read access to all patients, with the prompt instructing the model to only discuss the requesting clinician's patients. The security review's finding: a prompt injection could expose any record, because nothing downstream enforces scope. The fix exchanged each clinician's session for a token scoped to their permissions, so the FHIR API itself rejects out-of-scope reads. Encryption, logging, and prompt rules were all secondary — none of them constrain what a compromised session can reach.

examples.title: The email assistant as confused deputy
examples.body: An executive assistant agent read and sent mail with the executive's full privileges while summarizing messages from external senders. The threat model writes itself: an attacker emails hidden instructions, the agent processes them with real credentials, and mail is exfiltrated or sent in the executive's name. The remediation combined narrower scopes (read-only where possible), deterministic confirmation before any send action, and treating external content as untrusted data rather than instructions. The design lesson: trace where untrusted input enters and what credentials it can reach.

pitfalls: Treating prompt instructions as access control — the model can be talked out of instructions; authorization must be enforced by the API layer, which cannot.
Confusing authentication with authorization — MFA and mTLS strengthen identity and channel but do nothing to narrow what an authenticated session can access.
Relying on detective controls (logs, weekly reviews) as the primary safeguard — they find breaches after data has already left; preventive scoping must come first.
Believing credential rotation or secrets management fixes over-broad scope — a well-rotated admin key still reaches everything; lifetime and scope are independent properties.
Attributing actions to shared machine identities — compliance requires knowing which human's session drove each access, which means propagating end-user identity downstream.

objectives.objective: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
objectives.explanation:
Every Claude integration has a handful of dials that trade accuracy against latency and cost: model tier, extended thinking budget, retrieval depth (top-k), reranking stages, and how many chunks or tool results enter context. There is no universally correct setting — the architect's job is to justify each configuration against the specific use case's SLA and the cost of being wrong. A discharge-summary pipeline reviewed the next morning should spend its loose latency budget on the most capable model and thorough retrieval; a mobile chat assistant with a one-second abandonment threshold should not.

Two distinctions do a lot of work in exam scenarios. First, perceived versus total latency: streaming makes long generations feel responsive by showing tokens immediately, and parallelizing independent tool calls and retrieval cuts time-to-first-token — often delivering the responsiveness win that teams mistakenly buy with a model downgrade. Second, uniform versus routed configuration: when a workload mixes easy and hard requests, route the easy majority to a fast, cheap path and reserve the heavy configuration for the cases that need it, rather than degrading or gold-plating everything uniformly.

Finally, changes to these dials should be justified with measurement, not anecdote. Sweep the parameter (retrieval depth, model tier) against a representative eval set, quantify quality at each setting, and choose the cheapest configuration that clears the quality bar. 'It still looked fine in a few spot checks' is not an engineering justification, and neither is reflexively refusing to reduce a setting that measurement shows is past its point of diminishing returns.
objectives.whyItMatters: Misjudged trade-offs fail in both directions in production: over-provisioned pipelines burn budget and miss latency SLAs users actually feel, while blanket downgrades quietly raise error rates on the requests where mistakes are expensive. Architects are routinely asked to defend these settings to product, finance, and risk stakeholders, and 'we measured quality across configurations against the SLA' is the only defensible answer.

examples.title: Routing a bimodal workload
examples.body: A retail chatbot ran every request — 80% simple order-status lookups, 20% complex policy disputes — through a top-tier model with extended thinking and deep retrieval, hitting 9 seconds p95 against a 3-second SLA. Uniformly downgrading would sacrifice dispute quality; streaming alone would mask, not meet, the SLA. The fix routed simple intents to a fast small-model path with shallow retrieval and kept the heavy configuration for disputes. Latency and cost fell where the workload was easy, and accuracy held where being wrong was expensive.

examples.title: Spending headroom on accuracy
examples.body: A benefits office's overnight extraction pipeline finished in two hours of an eight-hour window using a fast model, and caseworkers spent mornings fixing errors. The team briefly considered finishing even faster with more workers. The better trade recognized the six spare hours as a resource: moving to a stronger model with fuller document context used more of the window and cut correction workload at the source. In batch pipelines with fixed deadlines, unused latency headroom should usually be converted into accuracy.

pitfalls: Optimizing total latency when the user only feels time-to-first-token — streaming and parallel calls often solve the perceived problem without any accuracy sacrifice.
Applying one configuration to a bimodal workload — uniform settings either overpay on easy requests or underserve hard ones; routing by difficulty serves both.
Chasing speed in pipelines with loose deadlines — an overnight batch that finishes early has wasted budget that could have bought accuracy.
Shipping retrieval or model-tier changes on spot checks — parameter changes need measured quality curves on an eval set, because degradation is often invisible in a handful of samples.
Assuming more retrieval is always better — beyond a workload-specific depth, extra chunks add latency and noise without recall gains; the curve must be measured, not presumed.

objectives.objective: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
objectives.explanation:
LLM observability spans three layers. Operational metrics — latency percentiles, error rates, token counts and cost, tagged by feature and tenant — should cover 100% of traffic; they are cheap and answer 'is the system up and what does it cost, and who is consuming it.' Content-level telemetry — prompts, completions, tool calls — is what engineers need to actually diagnose failures, but at scale it is expensive to store and sensitive to hold. The standard resolution is sampling: retain full traces for a random slice of traffic plus guaranteed capture of the conversations most likely to need investigation — errors, negative feedback, guardrail triggers.

Multi-step agents add a requirement that per-service logs cannot meet: trace-level visibility. An agent run is effectively a distributed transaction — plan, tool calls, intermediate outputs, final synthesis — and diagnosing a bad outcome requires one correlated trace linking every step under a workflow ID, exactly as distributed tracing does for microservices. Without it, engineers reconstruct timelines by hand across siloed systems.

Two further challenges recur. PII in logs: prompts and completions are a second copy of your most sensitive data flows, so redact or pseudonymize at ingestion, restrict and audit access, and enforce retention limits — and never rely on prompt instructions to keep sensitive data out of telemetry. And quality monitoring: dashboards full of latency and error metrics say nothing about whether answers are right. Production quality requires eval-in-production signals — user feedback controls (thumbs), periodic graded review of sampled real transcripts, and optionally scheduled scoring against rubrics — treated as first-class monitored metrics.
objectives.whyItMatters: At production scale, the failure mode is not too little data but the wrong data: teams drown in operational metrics while being unable to replay the one conversation a customer complained about, or discover during an audit that engineers could search raw PHI in logs. Quality regressions from model updates, data migrations, or prompt changes are invisible to uptime dashboards and are routinely caught first by users unless production eval signals exist.

examples.title: Sampling design at two million conversations
examples.body: A SaaS assistant handling two million monthly conversations could no longer afford full trace storage, but engineers refused to debug blind. The design that balanced both: aggregate metrics on all traffic, full prompt/completion/tool traces for a random sample, and guaranteed retention for every errored or thumbs-down conversation. Cost scaled with the sample; investigations kept the traces they actually needed, because the conversations worth investigating were precisely the ones always captured.

examples.title: The migration the dashboards missed
examples.body: After a catalog migration, a retailer's support team insisted answer quality had dropped, but latency, error, and token dashboards were all green and the engineering team had no way to confirm or refute the claim. The gap was semantic: no user feedback signal and no sampled transcript review existed. Adding thumbs feedback plus a weekly graded sample of real conversations gave the team a quality time series — which promptly showed the regression concentrated in migrated catalog categories, something no operational metric could ever surface.

pitfalls: Assuming green operational dashboards mean the system is working — latency and error metrics cannot detect wrong answers; quality needs its own signals.
Logging everything forever or nothing at all — the scalable position is metrics for all traffic, sampled deep traces, and guaranteed capture of failures and bad feedback.
Debugging multi-step agents from siloed per-service logs — without a correlated end-to-end trace, step-level diagnosis becomes days of manual timeline stitching.
Treating logs as less sensitive than production data — prompts and completions replicate PII into a store often more widely accessible than the source systems.
Relying on user complaints as the quality signal — users underreport and distrust silently; sampled evaluation of live traffic finds regressions complaints miss.

objectives.objective: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
objectives.explanation:
Chunking determines what the model can ever see intact, so it is where RAG accuracy is won or lost first. Fixed-size chunks are easy but split semantic units mid-clause; when documents have real structure — sections, clauses, headings — chunk along those boundaries, with overlap where units cross-reference. Chunk size itself is a precision/recall trade: small chunks embed precisely but strip surrounding context; large chunks carry context but dilute their embeddings across topics. The small-to-big pattern resolves the tension by decoupling the matching unit from the reading unit — index small chunks for precise similarity search, then expand hits to their parent section before passing them to the model.

Chunks also lose meaning when isolated from their documents: 'restart the service' retrieved without knowing which product or version it describes is ambiguous to both retriever and model. Contextual retrieval fixes this at ingestion by prepending each chunk's document and section context (product, version, topic) before embedding. Similarly, attach structured metadata — document type, department, version, effective date — so query-time filters can enforce category and freshness, which embedding similarity fundamentally cannot.

On the retrieval side, robust pipelines layer mechanisms. Embeddings handle paraphrase and semantic queries; lexical search (BM25) handles exact identifiers, error codes, and rare terms that embeddings represent poorly. Hybrid search merges candidates from both, and a reranking stage then rescores that high-recall pool directly against the query so only the most relevant chunks enter context. The pattern is recall-oriented retrieval first, precision-oriented reranking second.
objectives.whyItMatters: RAG quality failures in production almost always trace back to pipeline design choices — truncated clauses, context-free chunks, missing lexical matching, no version filtering — rather than to the model. These are expensive to retrofit because fixing chunking or enrichment means re-processing and re-indexing the corpus, so the architecture decisions this objective covers are cheapest to get right before launch.

examples.title: Clauses, not token counts
examples.body: An insurer's policy RAG chunked at a fixed 512 tokens and adjusters got wrong answers about coverage exceptions because retrieved chunks began or ended mid-clause. Shrinking chunks split clauses more often; enlarging them mixed several clauses per embedding. The fix chunked along the documents' own structure — sections and clauses — with overlap where provisions referenced each other, so an exception was always retrieved attached to the provision it modifies. Chunking strategy should mirror document structure whenever structure exists.

examples.title: Hybrid plus rerank for mixed queries
examples.body: A payments team's runbook assistant faced queries split between exact error codes ('PSP-4092') and loose paraphrases ('payouts stuck'). Pure vector search missed the identifier queries — codes are near-arbitrary strings embeddings handle poorly — and relevant chunks often ranked below marginal ones. Adding a BM25 index merged with vector candidates fixed identifier recall, and a reranker rescoring the merged pool fixed ordering. Neither addition alone covered both failure modes; the layered design did.

pitfalls: Tuning chunk size when the real problem is chunk boundaries — no fixed size fixes splitting semantic units; structural chunking does.
Indexing chunks stripped of document context — a chunk that cannot identify its own product, version, or section is ambiguous no matter how good the embedding model is.
Relying on embeddings for exact identifiers and codes — these are lexical-match problems, and hybrid search exists precisely because vectors handle them poorly.
Using similarity alone to handle category and recency — 'most similar' happily returns the wrong department's document or an outdated version; metadata filters enforce what geometry cannot.
Skipping reranking when candidates retrieve but rank poorly — retrieval optimizes recall over a large index; a reranker is the precision layer that decides what actually enters context.

objectives.objective: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
objectives.explanation:
Vector search is one retrieval mechanism, not the default. The first question is the data's shape. Structured records — transactions, inventories, tickets with fields — want deterministic query interfaces (SQL or APIs) that filter and aggregate exactly; exporting them as prose for embedding replaces exact answers with probabilistic recall, which is unacceptable when the question is 'what was the total.' Long-form prose fits embedded indexes well. Small, stable corpora — an FAQ of a few dozen thousand tokens — often need no retrieval at all: include everything in the prompt with caching, and there is no retrieval miss to debug.

The second question is the query pattern. Keyword-heavy queries — part numbers, error codes, SKUs, exact names — favor lexical or exact matching, because identifiers are near-arbitrary strings that embeddings represent poorly and that must never fuzzy-match to a neighbor. Semantic paraphrase queries — symptoms, descriptions, 'how do I' — favor embeddings. Real workloads usually mix both, which argues for routing by detected query pattern or for hybrid retrieval; analyzing actual query logs is how you find the mix.

The third question is freshness. A pre-built index is a snapshot: fine for policies that change quarterly, wrong for seat availability that changes by the minute — real-time state must come from the system of record at query time. The same logic favors agentic search (grep, file navigation, live API calls) over pre-indexed stores when the corpus changes faster than any re-indexing cadence, as with a busy codebase. Mixed corpora should be segmented by volatility, with each segment served by the mechanism its change rate demands.
objectives.whyItMatters: Teams that own a vector store tend to route every retrieval problem through it, producing systems that miscount transactions, confuse part numbers, and confidently report yesterday's availability. Matching mechanism to data shape and query pattern is frequently the difference between a system users trust and one they learn to double-check — and the wrong choice is usually invisible in demos and obvious in production.

examples.title: Transactions are not documents
examples.body: A bank considered exporting transaction histories into its existing vector store so the assistant could answer 'total card spend in March.' The architect redirected: aggregates and filters over structured records need exact semantics, and similarity search can silently miss rows — a wrong total is worse than no answer in finance. The agent instead received a parameterized query tool over the transaction database, turning each question into a deterministic filtered aggregation. Existing infrastructure convenience never outranks the data's shape.

examples.title: Segmenting by freshness
examples.body: A travel assistant served both bag-fee policy questions and seat-availability questions from one nightly-refreshed vector store, and availability answers were routinely wrong. No refresh cadence rescues minute-level volatility, and caveating stale answers still fails the traveler. The fix segmented by volatility: the embedded index kept serving slow-changing policy prose, while availability questions became live API calls to the inventory system. One corpus, two mechanisms, each matched to its data's rate of change.

pitfalls: Defaulting to vector search because the pipeline already exists — the data's shape and the query pattern choose the mechanism, not the team's sunk infrastructure.
Embedding structured data to answer aggregate or filtered questions — similarity retrieval is probabilistic, and totals, counts, and joins demand deterministic queries.
Building a full RAG pipeline for a small stable corpus — if everything fits in a cached prompt, retrieval adds engineering cost plus a recall failure mode for zero benefit.
Ignoring freshness when selecting retrieval — a perfect index of stale data gives confidently wrong answers about anything that changes faster than the refresh cadence.
Skipping query-log analysis — the split between identifier queries and paraphrase queries determines whether lexical, semantic, or hybrid retrieval fits, and it can only be measured, not assumed.

objectives.objective: Evaluate connection protocols and select the integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
objectives.explanation:
Three integration mechanisms cover most Claude architectures, and each has a regime where it wins. MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how clients discover and invoke tools and resources: implement a server once and any MCP-compatible client — Claude Code, the desktop app, custom applications — can use it without per-client integration code. Its second superpower is dynamic discovery: clients enumerate a server's tools at connection time, so newly published capabilities reach every connected assistant without a client release. Choose MCP when multiple clients need the same capabilities, or when the capability catalog grows independently of client deployments.

Direct API or CLI integration is the simplest mechanism and the right one when code orchestrates a fixed workflow with a single consumer — a batch pipeline calling Claude for classification, a service invoking a model step deterministically. Wrapping such flows in MCP servers adds surface to build, secure, and operate with no consumer to justify it; 'architectural consistency' is not a requirement.

Agent-to-agent delegation hands a task to another agent that owns the relevant expertise — its tools plus the prompts, reasoning, and guardrails engineered around them. Choose it when the unit of reuse is judgment, not capability: importing another team's tools transfers instruments without competence, and reimplementing their domain logic duplicates their hardest work and drifts. Delegation preserves ownership boundaries — the expert team keeps evolving their agent, and consumers integrate its conclusions. Its costs are real: an extra model-mediated hop adds latency, cost, and nondeterminism, so never use an agent hop to proxy what a plain tool call can do.
objectives.whyItMatters: Protocol choice determines integration economics as an organization scales: per-client custom wiring multiplies engineering cost with every new client, monolithic uniform standards add operational surface where none is needed, and transplanting tools without their guardrails creates safety gaps between teams. The exam tests whether you select by consumer count, reuse needs, ecosystem, and ownership — not by fashion.

examples.title: One server, five clients
examples.body: A pharma company had wired its document vault, LIMS, and compliance tracker directly into one application, and now faced demand from Claude Code, the desktop app, an internal chat tool, and two planned clients. Rewiring each integration into each client meant fifteen-plus custom paths. Implementing each integration once as an MCP server let every current and future client connect through the standard protocol — and dynamic discovery meant later capability additions required no client releases. Consumer count made the decision.

examples.title: Delegating to the expert agent
examples.body: An enrollment assistant needed financial-aid support, and a separate team already ran a production financial-aid agent with its own tools, regulatory reasoning, and guardrails. Importing the tools would transfer capability without the competence built around them; reimplementing the reasoning would duplicate and drift. Delegating financial-aid questions to the existing agent and relaying its conclusions reused the whole engineered package while each team kept ownership of its domain. Agent-to-agent fits when the value is in the other agent's judgment, not just its tools.

pitfalls: Standardizing every integration on MCP for consistency — a single code-orchestrated consumer is better served by a direct API call; MCP earns its surface through reuse and discovery.
Hand-wiring the same capability into each client — this rebuilds per-client what MCP implements once, and the cost multiplies with every client the organization adds.
Importing another agent's tools instead of delegating to it — tools without their surrounding prompts and guardrails are capability without competence, and safety properties do not transfer.
Routing simple tool calls through an orchestrator agent — a model-mediated hop adds latency, cost, and nondeterminism that a direct call avoids; delegate tasks, not lookups.

Forgetting dynamic discovery when capabilities grow independently of clients — build-time bindings (SDKs, custom adapters) force a redeploy per new capability, which MCP's runtime enumeration eliminates.

objectives.objective: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
objectives.explanation:
Monolithic context loads everything upfront — every tool definition, every document — so the model always has full visibility with zero extra round-trips. Progressive discovery starts lean and loads on demand: a small core toolset plus a mechanism to pull in tool definitions when the task needs them, or a lightweight index (titles, parties, dates) with full content fetched as questions require. Each strategy has a real cost: monolithic context pays tokens and attention dilution on every request — hundreds of definitions or hundreds of thousands of document tokens measurably degrade selection accuracy and clause-level answers even when most are irrelevant to the task at hand — while discovery pays round-trip latency, added machinery, and new failure modes whenever something must be fetched.

The decision rule is the ratio of catalog size to per-task usage. When tasks touch a small slice of a large catalog — an IT-ops agent with 300 tools where conversations use one or two systems, a legal assistant over dozens of contracts where questions concern one — discovery's occasional round-trips buy large token and attention savings on every request. When a small, stable set is used constantly — a support agent's six tools invoked all day — upfront loading is simpler, faster, and equally accurate, and discovery machinery would add complexity for nothing.

Beware of fixes that treat one symptom of monolithic bloat while leaving the rest: prompt caching amortizes the recurring token cost of a stable prefix but cached definitions still fill the window and still dilute attention; compressing descriptions saves tokens but strips the detail the model needs to use tools correctly; splitting into per-system agents shrinks each context but pushes the routing problem onto users and breaks cross-system tasks.
objectives.whyItMatters: Context strategy decides an agent platform's scaling behavior: monolithic loading makes every added connector or document degrade every conversation slightly, until cost and accuracy problems appear with no single obvious cause. Conversely, teams that cargo-cult discovery onto small stable toolsets ship latency and operational complexity for zero benefit. Architects must place each agent in the correct regime and re-evaluate as its catalog grows.

examples.title: 300 tools, two used
examples.body: An IT-operations agent injected roughly 300 tool definitions from 14 connectors into every conversation; baseline context was huge and tool-selection accuracy declined with each connector added, though most conversations used one or two systems. Compression would strip the guidance the model needs; caching would cut cost but not the attention dilution; per-system agents would dump routing on users. The fix was a lean core plus on-demand loading of each system's definitions when the task called for them — paying rare discovery round-trips to reclaim tokens and attention on every request.

examples.title: Six tools, leave them loaded
examples.body: A food-delivery support agent used exactly six stable tools, all invoked constantly. An engineer proposed a discovery layer citing context-efficiency best practices. The assessment: six definitions cost negligible tokens and cause no selection ambiguity, so discovery would add round-trip latency and operational machinery with nothing to save. Upfront loading with the stable block prompt-cached was correct. The principle applied without its preconditions — a large catalog with sparse usage — is just imported complexity.

pitfalls: Treating progressive discovery as universally superior — with a small, heavily used toolset there is nothing meaningful to save, and discovery adds latency and failure modes for free.
Assuming prompt caching fixes monolithic bloat — caching amortizes token cost of a stable prefix, but cached content still occupies the window and still dilutes the model's attention.
Compressing tool descriptions to fit more in — the description detail is what drives correct selection and parameterization, so compression trades the bloat problem for an accuracy problem.
Splitting an overloaded agent per system to shrink context — this pushes routing onto users who don't know which system a task touches and breaks cross-system tasks entirely.

Loading whole corpora because 'the model should see everything' — beyond the token cost, mostly irrelevant content measurably degrades answers; an index upfront with on-demand fetch concentrates attention where the task needs it.
